licenses.name: Name
licenses.author: Author
licenses.note: Piece sets come from github.com/lichess-org/lila (public/piece), listed in its COPYING.md. Sets with a non-commercial or unclear license are left out. The sounds are made by the app's own code, and the knight icon is your own design.

games: Stockfish goes through every move of these games to find mistakes and best moves. Fewer games make the first check faster; the other games still count in results and ratings.
depth: For each position of your games, Stockfish looks at this many positions before it decides. More means fewer wrong verdicts, but more time. It's a fixed amount of work, so fast and slow processor cores give the same quality.
workers: Each copy of Stockfish uses one processor core (this computer has {cores}). 4 is the tested default: fast enough, and the laptop stays cooler and quieter.
nightly: Windows runs the update every night: new games, Stockfish, puzzles and the phone app. It waits until the computer has been idle for 10 minutes, so never while you play.
note: Once a week a small AI model on this computer (Ollama) writes 2-4 short points from your weekly numbers, in Egyptian Arabic. Every number in it is checked against your data. Nothing goes online.
temperature: How often the bot plays a less likely move instead of its favorite. Higher means more surprising moves. {tuned} was the closest match to your real games in the 25 November test.
cutoff: Moves the model finds much less likely than its favorite (under this share of its chance) are never played, so the bot doesn't make random-looking moves.
maia_rating: Base Maia-3 was trained on millions of human games and plays like a person of this rating (Lichess scale, a bit higher than chess.com).
pz_today: Positions from your own games where you made a big mistake or missed a brilliant move. Find the best move: the board checks it against Stockfish's answer.
pz_new: {per_day} new puzzles a day from your games of the last {days} days, newest first. When you finish them, you can ask for more.
pz_due: A puzzle you got wrong comes back after 1 day, then after 3 days, then after a week. Solve it at the one-week review and it counts as learned.
top_motif: Of your big mistakes in the last 4 weeks made with 10 seconds or more on your clock, the most common kind: {motif}.
focus: Your one thing to work on
The first weakness in your coach's notes, and the number from the notes that shows whether it's getting better, counted over your last 4 weeks. It changes when your coach writes new notes.
plan: Your coach's weekly plan has a few tasks for each day of the week. Tick them off as you go; the ticks start fresh tomorrow.
converted: Games where Stockfish gave you an 80% or better chance to win at some point (about 4 pawns ahead), and how many of them you went on to win. Your coach's goal is {goal}.
late_blunders: A big mistake (a blunder) drops your chance to win by 15 points or more. This counts them per 100 of your moves after move 10, only while the game was still open (20-80% chance to win). Lower is better; your coach's goal is {goal}.
abandoned: The share of games you left (closed or stopped playing) before they ended. Lower is better; your coach's goal is {goal}.
accuracy: How close your moves were to Stockfish's best moves, from 0 to 100, with the formula Lichess publishes. Your coach's goal is {goal}.
top_motif_rate: Your most common mistake, per 100 moves
How often you made your most common kind of big mistake, per 100 moves made with 10 seconds or more. Lower is better; your coach's goal is {goal}.
win_chance: Stockfish's evaluation turned into a chance from 0% to 100%: 50% is equal, a pawn up is about 59%, three pawns about 75%.
blind: The app secretly picks Gojo bot or base Maia-3 (both play your book moves in the opening, so only the network differs). After the game you guess which one it was, and say whether it played entirely like you. Guessing right much more than half the time means Gojo bot really plays differently.
book: In positions you reached at least 3 times, the bot plays one of your real moves there, the recent ones counting more. Elsewhere the trained model picks a move.
accuracy_game: How close your moves in this game were to Stockfish's best moves, from 0 to 100. Games Stockfish hasn't checked yet have none.
blunders_game: Your moves in this game that dropped your chance to win by 15 points or more.
best_game: ‼ Brilliant (a sacrifice that works) and ! Great (the only good move) moves you played in this game.
trend_blunders: Moves after move 10 that dropped your chance to win by 15 points or more, per 100 such moves, counted only while the game was still open. Lower is better.
trend_converted: Of the games where Stockfish gave you an 80% or better chance to win at some point, the share you won. Higher is better.
trend_abandoned: The share of games you left before they ended. Lower is better.
pz_first: Puzzles you solved on your first try, out of the ones you tried.
pz_learned: Puzzles you got wrong at first and then solved at the one-week review.

review.phone: My games works in the app on the laptop (the phone shows the summaries).
review.chart: Your chance to win, move by move

results: How many games you won, drew and lost: all together, with White and with Black, and in each time control.
ratings: Your chess.com rating at the end of each day you played, for rated games. A flat stretch means you didn't play that time control then.
accuracy: How close your moves were to Stockfish's best moves, from 0 to 100, with the formula Lichess publishes. About 1 point higher than chess.com's Game Review on average.
phases: Big mistakes per 100 of your moves in the opening (moves 1-10), the middlegame and the endgame (6 or fewer queens, rooks, bishops and knights left). Only moves made while the game was still open count (20-80% chance to win): once a game is decided, nothing can be called a big mistake.
clock: How often you make a big mistake depending on how much time you had left when the move started. The opening isn't counted: you nearly always have time there.
motifs: What kind of big mistake each one was, read from Stockfish's best line: a piece left where it can be taken for free, a fork, a pin, a missed mate, and so on. A pattern only counts when its line really wins material.
best: Brilliant: a sacrifice that works (you give up material and you're still fine). Great: the only good move in the position (every other move would have been a big mistake). Your opponents' moves are judged by the same rules.
reel: Your best Brilliant and Great moves, at most one per game, each on a board seen from your side. The arrow is the move.
missed: Positions where a brilliant sacrifice was the best move, and you played a move that cost at least 10 points of your chance to win instead.
openings: Your results in the openings you play most, with White and with Black. Lighter numbers rest on few games, so they can swing a lot.
drops: In each opening you played 150+ times, the move after which your score falls the most, and whether Stockfish thinks that move itself is bad (only when your chance to win falls by 5+ points).
endings: For wins, what happened to your opponent (checkmate, time, resigned, left); for losses, what happened to you.
ends: Games decided on time or by leaving
Where you stood when a game ended on time or because someone left: winning, about equal or losing. In bullet the clock decides many games from both sides.
hours: How many games you play at each hour, and whether you win more or less than usual at that hour.
tilt: Your win rate right after losing several games in a row in the same session (a break of 30 minutes starts a new session), and how you do as a session goes on.
rating-diff: Your score against opponents rated above or below you (a draw counts half), next to what the rating difference predicts.
coach: Written in Egyptian Arabic by Claude from your numbers. Every number in the text must be one of your real numbers: the chips under each paragraph show where it comes from, and the notes are checked before they show.

games: How many games are counted here.
win rate: The share of these games you won.
your accuracy: How close your moves were to Stockfish's best, from 0 to 100, averaged over these games.
centipawn loss per move: How much worse than Stockfish's best move your moves were on average, in hundredths of a pawn. Lower is better.
blunders: A move that drops your chance to win by 15 points or more.
mistakes: A move that drops your chance to win by 10 to 15 points.
made in time trouble: Big mistakes made with less than 10 seconds on your clock.
your top motif: The most common kind of big mistake in the last 4 weeks, made with 10+ seconds on your clock.
brilliant moves: Sacrifices that work: you give up material and you are still fine afterwards. Per 100 games.
great moves: The only good move in the position: every other move would have been a big mistake.
missed brilliants: Positions where a brilliant sacrifice was the best move and you played something else that cost 10+ points.
win rate in games with your brilliant: How often you won the games in which you played a Brilliant move.
in total: All of them together, in these games.

progress.trends_intro: Each point counts your last 4 weeks up to that week, so one bad day doesn't swing it. The dashed line is your coach's goal.
progress.chart_blunders: Big mistakes per 100 moves after the opening
progress.few: Few games those weeks: the line can swing.
progress.pz_none: Nothing tried yet in this app: your progress shows here after your first puzzle. (Your phone keeps its own progress.)
progress.pz_note: The real sign that the training works is in your games: the trend of your most common mistake (Trends).
